hints: Start by looking at size and position in Fig. 1.1. One label points to a large grainy region at the top of the cell, one points to a dark lens-shaped body at the edge, and one points to the huge pale space filling the middle.
Think about which structure stores DNA and controls the cell, which structure carries out photosynthesis in a leaf, and which structure is filled with cell sap and pushes the cytoplasm to the edge.
Match X to the granular control centre with dark chromatin, Y to the photosynthetic organelle with starch grains inside, and Z to the fluid-filled central compartment.
walkthrough:
Reading X at the top of the cell**
X is the large region with granular material and dark patches of chromatin. That texture is typical of the nucleus, which contains DNA and controls cell activities.

Reading Y around the edge**
Y points to dark, oval bodies arranged around the periphery. In a leaf cell these are chloroplasts, the sites of photosynthesis. You can even see pale starch grains stored inside them.

Reading Z in the centre**
Z points to the very large, pale, almost empty-looking area filling most of the cell. That is the large permanent vacuole filled with cell sap, typical of a mature plant cell.
Final answer: X - nucleus; Y - chloroplast; Z - (large permanent) vacuole.

hints: List the three big plant-only features you can see in Fig. 1.1 - the rigid outer layer, the green photosynthetic bodies, and the huge central fluid sac - then ask which of these an animal cell would lack.
Remember you need two separate structural differences, and for the vacuole point you must stress large and permanent, since animal cells may have only small temporary vacuoles.
walkthrough:
Thinking plant-only structures**
Mature plant cells have a cellulose cell wall outside the membrane, many chloroplasts for photosynthesis, and one large permanent vacuole containing cell sap. Animal cells do not have any of these in that form.

Picking two clear differences**
A good pair is: animal cells have no chloroplasts, and have no large permanent vacuole, at most small temporary vacuoles. Alternatively, animal cells have no cell wall and have centrioles, which plant cells lack.

Final answer: Any two from: no large permanent vacuole, only small temporary vacuoles; no chloroplasts; no cell wall, only cell surface membrane; no plasmodesmata; centrioles present; nucleus more central, not pushed to periphery.

hints: Recall the standard food test that turns dark only when coiled amylose is present to trap the test ions inside its helix.
Remember the starting colour of that reagent in the bottle is orange-brown, so state both the reagent name and the start to end colour for full credit.
walkthrough:
Naming the reagent**
Starch is tested with iodine solution, often called iodine in potassium iodide solution. It is added directly to the sample.

Seeing the positive result**
Iodine solution is orange-brown. If starch is present, iodine molecules fit inside the amylose helix and the colour changes to deep blue-black, sometimes described as blue, black or purple.
Final answer: reagent: iodine solution (iodine in potassium iodide); colour change: orange / brown to blue / black / purple if starch present.

hints: Start from the monomer level - both molecules are polysaccharides built from the same type of glucose, so think which form of glucose and which type of bond joins them.
Now focus on the 1-4 linkages that both share to make chains, then ask what extra type of linkage creates side branches in only one of them.
Picture the 3D shape - one molecule stays as a long coiled chain while the other forms a branched bush-like molecule, so compare unbranched versus branched and helical versus non-helical.
For a 4-mark compare, aim for about two similarities and two differences with paired detail, including bond positions 1-4 and 1-6 and relative size or compactness.
walkthrough:
Establishing the similarities**
Both amylose and amylopectin are polysaccharides of starch. Both are polymers of alpha-glucose joined by glycosidic bonds formed by condensation. Both contain 1-4 glycosidic bonds linking glucose in straight chains.

Contrasting branching**
Amylose is unbranched, a single straight chain that coils into a helix. Amylopectin is branched, with side chains attached by additional 1-6 glycosidic bonds at branch points, giving a more bush-like and compact molecule.

Adding size and shape detail**
Because it is unbranched, amylose is the smaller molecule and its helical shape is what traps iodine in the starch test. Amylopectin is larger overall but more compact for storage because of extensive branching, allowing many ends for rapid hydrolysis.

Final answer: Similarities: both are polymers / polysaccharides; both made of alpha-glucose monomers; monomers joined by glycosidic bonds; both contain 1-4 glycosidic bonds. Differences: amylose unbranched, amylopectin branched; amylopectin has additional 1-6 glycosidic bonds at branch points; amylose is helical and smaller, amylopectin is more compact / larger branched molecule.
